title_original: Steps review – Netflix’s Disney-lite Cinderella rework has enough pep in its step
excerpt_original: The plot might be a little overstuffed and the animation style could be a little more distinctive, but this is better than the streamer’s average animated offering Stop me if you’ve heard this one before, but that age-old story you think you know, well, you might not know it at…

blocks.text: S top me if you’ve heard this one before, but that age-old story you think you know, well, you might not know it at all. It’s a tale as old as Shrek, which was by no means the first film to subvert fairytale expectations, but it was definitely the most influential, and we’re still feeling its impact 25 years later, for better or worse. What if that villain wasn’t actually the villain after all? What if that love interest shouldn’t have been of interest in the first place? What if that damsel in distress was given a bullet-speed fight scene instead of weeping in a tower?

But what might have seemed fresh in 2001, if not quite as fresh for anyone who knew and loved The Princess Bride , has grown a little tiresome ever since. Bucking the conventions has essentially become the convention, and effortful attempts to remix classic storytelling beats have mostly ended up reeking of smugness. Yet they still keep coming (IP is king) and before the inevitable Shrek legacy sequel hits cinemas next summer, Netflix is trying to conjure up that same mix of snark and sentiment with Steps, a Cinderella story but, wait for it, not the Cinderella story you thought you knew …

While the existence of yet another rule-rewriting storybook rework might not be a surprise, the fact that Steps is mostly rather watchable actually is. It’s not just because of the low bar set by this particular subgenre but also by the streamer’s animated output thus far. Too much of it feels like either off-brand Disney or knock-off DreamWorks, from Spellbound to Swapped to In Your Dreams , and while Steps doesn’t entirely avoid that same trap, its lack of originality is made up for by just about enough pep.

With the requisite storybook opening that is interrupted by the “actually wait” reminder that this tale is, again, not what you expected it would be , Steps starts by having Lilith (voiced by Ali Wong) try to clear something up. The legend might have painted her as an “evil stepsister” to poor Cinderella, but that’s not quite how it went down (the title refers to having a step rather than a biological sister). Lilith and her sister Margot (Stephanie Hsu) had initially tried to foster a relationship with Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried, having quite the varied run), but tensions grew as the more privileged and socially accepted blond stepsister chose the in-crowd over her blended family.

Years later, it’s still the assumptions of others that have demonised the sisters, especially Lilith, who has responded by leaning into her punk persona, listening to Olivia Rodrigo (OK pop-punk persona) and choosing purples and blacks over the pastels of the women around her. When the begrudging prince (Daniel Radcliffe) is forced by his parents to take a bride, a ball is planned and Cinderella’s secret Fairy Godmother (a perfectly cast Bette Midler) reveals herself to help. But magic is thrown from wrong hand to wrong hand and disaster strikes, leaving the three spurned from the kingdom with one turned into a frog and an evil rival (Nikki Glaser, excellent at playing mean girl) fooling the prince into thinking she’s his match.

What follows is a pretty familiar quest narrative as the stepsisters must make their way back to fix it all while also fixing their relationship. Although as straightforward as the structure might be, the plot gets a little overly busy and the film sometimes strains under the pressure of all that’s going on. It came from an idea originated by comedy duo Garfunkel and Oates, but it’s since gone through multiple revisions, a process that was allegedly far from ideal , and one can feel the work of too many hands fiddling with an increasingly convoluted script. There’s time travel, trolls, evil dolls, a second romantic subplot and lessons about sisterhood, empathy, and vaguely, racial harmony (the sisters are Asian American in a kingdom that’s overwhelmingly white). In a number of these not-the-story-you-know spins, there can often be a tendency to overdo the reinvention, and while Cinderella is a basic and regressive tale (expanding the 74-minute Disney original to 105 minutes in the live-action remake was a tiring stretch), one misses the simple elegance of what was at stake and how it unfolded.

But when the focus is kept tighter, Steps is a sprightly and at times surprisingly amusing adventure that, in its relentless desire to keep us on our feet, is at the very least never dull. It comes from Amy Poehler’s production company, which last partnered with Netflix for her spunky and charming teen comedy Moxie (one of the streamer’s best YA movies), and while this doesn’t teach inspiring lessons for younger female viewers in quite the same skillful way, there’s a similarly sharp sense of humour. There are some decent quips and neat ideas (the prince has face blindness, which we see through his eyes as emoji smiley faces; the villain’s ghoulish yet loving longtime henchman is desperate to be more of a father figure), and while the animated style could benefit from a lick of something more distinctive, less in thrall to what’s come before, it does at least look considerably less tinny than Netflix’s god-awful Thanksgiving 2024 offering Spellbound .

There’s also a considerable boost in energy from a spirited voice cast, and there’s a wise decision to focus more on a zippy teen pop soundtrack (original songs from Jennie and Rose Gray) over anonymous musical numbers (there’s just one and it’s used as more of a parody). We’re nowhere close to Disney vintage (although this is much better than the studio’s last sorry attempt to hard launch a princess ), but this is a step in the right direction.
